title.narrative: SRHR Next Joint leadership for stronger rights and better health

description.narrative:
The Dutch SRHR Alliance is a bold new two-and-a-half-year Pilot programme in which 11 Dutch organisations join forces with local partners in eight countries in Africa and the Middle East.
Together, they want to make sure that women, young people and marginalised groups have acces to SRHR care and services and can make well-informed and healthy choices about sex, relationships and having children – safely, freely and with good healthcare.
Why is this needed? Worldwide, funding for sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) is being cut. Clinics close, contraceptives run out, and the most vulnerable people loose access to care. At the same time, powerful anti-rights movements try to roll back hard-won freedoms. This programme is a direct answer to that crisis.
The Alliance will focus on three things. First, keeping essential SRHR services open and improving them: from contraception and safe childbirth care to HIV services and support for survivors of sexual violence. Second, giving young people and communities clear, honest and inclusive information about sexuality, consent and rights, both offline and via digital tools. Third, creating an environment where SRHR is more understood and accepted – by working with parents, community leaders, journalists, influencers and even private companies to challenge harmful norms and misinformation.
What makes this programme truly innovative is how it is organised. Instead of 11 Dutch organisations each running their own project, they act as one coordinated Alliance. They share knowledge, tools and data, avoid duplication and speak with a strong, common voice towards governments and international partners. A dedicated Innovation, Expertise & Research Hub collects lessons from many countries, tests new ideas (such as digital health solutions or new ways of working with the private sector) and spreads what works quickly across the Alliance.
Equally innovative is the strong focus on localisation. Local organisations are not just “implementers”; they are in the lead. In each of the eight countries, a partner platform of local civil society organisations will jointly decide on priorities, strategies and budgets. Dutch Country Support Partners provide backup and technical support, but decisions are made in country. At least 85% of all programme costs will be incurred by local organisations, and 80% of the total budget goes directly to work in the countries, not to overhead in the Netherlands.
The Alliance takes power balances seriously. It will develop a Localisation Charter, co-created with partners, and a tool to measure whether power and resources are really shifting. Youth, disability, women and key population led groups are actively involved in design, monitoring and learning. A risk sharing approach, inspired by the Dutch Relief Alliance (DRA), ensures that local partners are not burdened with responsibility without having a say.
A crucial first step is the five-month inception phase. In this start up period, Dutch embassies will be consulted for alignment with other Dutch funding in the respective eight countries. During the inception, the overall ToC will be tailored to local contexts. Country teams will map needs and risks and carry out capacity assessments. Each country alliance then co-creates its own theory of change, detailed workplan and budget, and agrees how responsibilities and funds are divided between partners. The monitoring, evaluation and learning framework – including indicators and a localisation “measuring tool” – is also finalised in this phase, so that progress can be tracked from the start.
In short, this programme aims to protect and expand access to SRHR services and information at a time of shrinking space and funding – and to do so in a new way: 11 Dutch organisations working as one, while putting local leadership, shared learning and innovation firmly at the centre.
